items.title: Deploying a .NET Application with Azure and Neon
items.description: A practical look at connecting an ASP.NET Core application to managed PostgreSQL and deploying the application to Azure.

sections.title: Why this setup
paragraphs: The goal was to move a database-backed .NET application beyond local development without introducing unnecessary infrastructure.
Using Azure for application hosting and Neon for managed PostgreSQL provided a practical way to deploy the application while keeping infrastructure management relatively small.

sections.title: Connecting PostgreSQL
paragraphs: The application needed a production database connection that was separate from local development configuration.
This meant treating connection strings and environment variables as deployment configuration rather than hard-coding them into the application.

sections.title: Moving to Azure
paragraphs: Deployment introduced issues that were not visible during local development, especially around environment configuration and external database connectivity.
Testing the complete deployed application was important because a successful build does not necessarily mean every production dependency is configured correctly.

sections.title: What I learned
paragraphs: Hosting and database configuration are part of application architecture rather than tasks that only happen after development.
Managed services such as Neon can reduce infrastructure complexity and make smaller applications easier to operate.

items.title: Orchestrating Python Automation from ASP.NET Core
items.description: How I separated application orchestration from browser automation in a local price monitoring system built with ASP.NET Core, Python and Playwright.

sections.title: Separating responsibilities
paragraphs: Price monitoring involves more than browser automation. The application also needs product configuration, scheduling, notifications, execution control and historical results.
Instead of putting those responsibilities into the scraper, I kept ASP.NET Core as the application layer and Python as the automation layer.

sections.title: ASP.NET Core as the orchestration layer
paragraphs: The ASP.NET Core application manages products, manual execution, email settings and scheduling while coordinating the Python scraper process.
This keeps application responsibilities separate from browser-specific extraction logic and makes the overall workflow easier to reason about.

sections.title: Designing for unreliable data
paragraphs: External websites can change independently of the application, so a scraper should not assume that every extracted value is correct.
The workflow includes validation, suspicious-change detection and diagnostic information so failed or unusual runs can be investigated.

sections.title: Why the scraper runs locally
paragraphs: Some monitored websites may restrict traffic from cloud data centers, so the scraper is intentionally designed to run locally rather than attempting to work around those restrictions.
Windows Task Scheduler provides scheduled execution while the application also supports manual runs.

sections.title: What I learned
paragraphs: Combining .NET and Python works well when each runtime has a clear responsibility.
Automation becomes more reliable when scheduling, validation, diagnostics, notifications and concurrency are treated as part of the application design rather than added later.

items.title: Building an AI Application with React, Python and Ollama
items.description: How a React frontend can communicate with a Python AI service and locally hosted language models through Ollama.

sections.title: Separating UI and AI logic
paragraphs: The React frontend should focus on the application experience rather than knowing how language models are executed.
Keeping model communication in a Python service creates a clearer boundary between interface code and AI-specific functionality.

sections.title: Using Ollama locally
paragraphs: Ollama provides a convenient way to experiment with language models locally during development.
Local execution makes it possible to test prompts, character behaviour and model integration before deciding whether a hosted AI provider is needed.

sections.title: Preparing for growth
paragraphs: The initial application can remain relatively small while the AI interaction is being explored.
As requirements grow, authentication, persistent conversations, users and application rules can move into a more complete backend and data model.

sections.title: What I learned
paragraphs: AI applications still benefit from conventional software architecture.
Separating model integration from frontend responsibilities makes it easier to change models, providers and application workflows later.
